posts.text:
everyone coding with agents should internalize this -

the RLVR in current frontier LLMs' post-training is done at task level. in other words, they won't give a damn about long term maintainability

this is why we see so many useless comments and test cases being written by default. these things make future tasks less efficient, but they don't affect the current task's success, so they survived the training and became part of the models' behaviors

until post-training can reward long term maintainability (which i suspect is very hard because inherently it's a slow and expensive process to measure that), it's on us humans to correct it in the harness layer through prompts, skills, lint rules etc

this also implies that understanding long term implications of technical choices is a valuable human skill that's hard for an average person to make up for with LLM

it's the distinction of whether you can create a durable growing codebase, or have one that gradually degrades  into insanity

if you have that skill, you are golden (for now, until post-training catches up)

posts.creator: kunchenguid
posts.text:
my PR count took a nose dive in the past week, from previously about 200 PRs/day to only 30-ish now, and i'm shipping more than ever

this happened because i started batching multiple branches into a single PR to improve CI efficiency

right now my CI architecture is -

1. each change gets developed in its own branch as usual

2. each branch that's done gets a very light weight CI check, mostly build and lint

3. all the branches that pass checks then get queued up into a batch

4. a batch becomes a PR which does a heavier CI job

5. while a PR of mine is still active, all new branches wait in the next batch, until the previous PR is merged. this means at any given point in time, in the same repo i will only have at most one PR at a time

6. if a PR fails CI, i fix forward with a new branch added into its batch. this means older branches, even if at fault, would remain immutable which minimizes rebases

so far, this has been working wonders. i think this is much superior than merge queues, because merge queues are typically done at a repo level, and at agent speed the queue can have hundreds of PRs at a time which breaks often and causes a lot of re-selection and makes everyone wait

this batching happens at user level, so different contributors in the same repo never have to interfere with each other. every user can also choose to apply different strategies - some users may do one PR per branch, and some may do this batch - and they can all work together

posts.text:
ok after a full day of using gpt 6.2 astra and sol on my real projects, here's my review

tl;dr - they are not a drop-in replacement for fable 5.2 and opus 5.5, but they are _really good_ once you figured out how to use their strength

1. first, the quirks

i started called these the "gpt smell", which is still here with the 6.2 series

the models' judgment on when to ask the user about something and when to go ahead is just not quite right. it'll escalate trivial decisions where clearly only one option is preferable, or choose to go down a path by itself that makes significant tradeoffs that should have needed my eyes

so as a primary driver for "let me just talk to it about everything" type of use case, they aren't great - i'd say they are close to opus 5 in this regard, and far behind opus 5.5

2. but... i found something _really_ cool

having ultrafast on sol is completely insane. with astra, it burns my wallet ultrafast, but with sol it's actually quite affordable! 

the best use of sol on ultrafast that i've found is adversarial code reviews - they typically don't need to run a lot of heavy tool calls that would slow them down. most of the time is spent on the model, which gets massively accelerated by ultrafast

once you got a feel from using sol ultrafast as the code reviewer, you can never go back. it feels like pure magic

3. and... i found something else that's really cool

we are not supposed to ask the gpt 6.2 series to respond in text. we should let them respond in html! (i use lavish-axi, but you can just ask for html or use whatever fits in your harness)

i suspect they are post-trained specifically on their latest "intelligent UI" concept in chatgpt - these models are so good at visual presentations of ideas

once you allow the model to respond in visual artifacts, it's a completely different game. the reports and decisions explained by astra in html is a clear step function better than what fable and opus give me

so after a day of use, i've made two changes to my setup:
- always sol ultrafast as code reviewer
- i started preferring asking astra for planning in html artifacts over fable/opus. i think i'll keep a/b testing for a while to decide how much and for which case i fully switch over

all in all, i strongly recommend spending more time with these two models. don't expect them to be the "everything" model, but rather figure out where they fit best in your workflow. i couldn't be happier for the two use cases i found above, and i'm pretty sure there are more

posts.text:
to start getting your CI under control, it's important to first understand there are a few different types of validations that exist

1. the code follows our rules
2. this change works
3. everything in the main branch works
4. the product is ready to release

traditionally, many codebases run all 4 on every PR as part of their CI pipeline. when every dev merges ~1 PR a day on average, that's doable

but as more and more people can merge 10s or 100s more PRs a day with effective use of agents, their CI starts to struggle. and buying more CI minutes or using faster CI is a losing battle

the solution is to 

- run only #1 and #2 on each PR

and #1 (mostly compile and lint) is typically fast enough that can run as pre-commit hooks as well

on each PR's CI pipeline, try to select only tests that are being edited and relevant to the change, because this is a high frequency bucket and you want to keep this extremely fast

consider assigning a fixed budget such as 5 minutes - whenever the pipeline exceeds that budget, ask an agent to optimize and get it back under the threshold

- run #3 using your merge queue or as a post-push rolling CI pipeline

this is typically your full test suite. running them on every PR at agent speed is simply too much overhead, but you also don't want to fully stop running the full suite, because some problems only occur when multiple changes combine

if you do this post-push, it means your main branch can have problems from time to time. counter-intuitively, that's okay. problems will exist no matter how many tests you run in your CI

when something breaks, fix forward. agents can do this very quickly. and you have a record of which commits pass the full suite - only create releases from those commits

- manage #4 using feature gates and phased rollouts

typically, you should get to a state where anything that could pass #3 is safe to release

in practice though, some problems will only happen with real traffic, so if you are running something at scale, you'd want some gates based on real telemetry

so the pipeline you could create is to release good commits to say 5% of your users, and progressively rollout further only when data looks good

once you have a clean separation of these 4 categories of gates, it'll be easy to know how to optimize and how to make tradeoffs between them

posts.text:
i found "executive mindset" to be the biggest differentiator from people who can use agents super effectively

it comes natural for people who had been an executive of a large org before, but it's counter-intuitive for people who haven't done so

a few examples

1. after you send a prompt, do you stare at the chat to see what the agent is doing?

most agent UX today leads people to do that, but a good executive never watches over an employee's shoulder after they've sent an ask - they are immediately on to the next problem

2. do you rely on chat for important decision making?

"just chat" sounds elegant, but there's a reason company executives rarely rely on plain talking for high stake decisions

instead, they ask the team for documents or presentations. it puts a bit more prep work on the team, but the discussions end up being a lot more efficient

3. when your agent did something wrong, do you curse at it and twist its arms to do it right?

some successful executives actually do that as well, but they also do something else afterwards - figure out what allowed the mistake to happen in the first place, and stop it at its root

4. do you spend all your time carefully examining everything to make sure the code is bug free?

now this is getting spicy, but you can pick any popular product on earth and you won't find a single one that's bug free

good executives accept the calculated risk and invest time in the right workflows to catch bugs early before shipping, get alerts if they happen, and making sure fixes can go out quickly - never make themselves the bottleneck by being the tester

our tools, skills, workflows etc change all the time, but building the right mindset is durable and can help you for a long time

if you aren't clear how to acquire the mindset yet, i recommend starting with asking yourself this when you try to decide to do something or not -

"if i have 100x more agents doing 100x more work for me every day, how would i do this?"

do this enough times, and you'll find yourself actually able to control 100x more agents effectively

overheard from friends talking about AI in China, and it’s very alarming

- AI short films went massive in China market because of how good the video models are now

- the first wave of people who mastered using AI to generate short films and comics made quite some money because they could produce a lot more content than traditional workflows

- but within just a few months, everybody and their mom could make equally good short films because all the expertise could be written in a markdown file

- when everyone’s more productive, no one actually has an advantage and it’s a race to the bottom. very quickly it became impossible to make money, and everyone’s busier than they were without AI

- the only one making money now is companies like bytedance who owns user demand and distribution. they sell ads to creators who pay to get traffic, and eventually ad spend became 80% of those creators’ operating expense, while AI tokens is less than 5%

so what are the problems here? 

1. there’s no moat if you are creating anything with AI

if a human is really good at something, and it’s hard to find more humans who can do the same, they can leverage the scarcity of their skill to get paid very well

but if AI is good at something, it will be infinitely replicated, so there’s no scarcity hence you can’t really expect a sustainable business by creating anything with AI

2. more creators created more content people actually liked. that’s a good thing

but the economical benefit of that all got absorbed by the distribution platforms

there’s a famous chinese poem 遍身罗绮者，不是养蚕人 - it basically says people who dress well aren’t the people making dresses. that’s exactly what’s happening here

if our society doesn’t figure out a better way to distribute wealth, AI will help billionaires become trillionaires while average people become more exhausted than ever

posts.text:
my open source projects collectively crossed 30k+ stars on github, going from almost zero just a few months ago! 🎉

reflecting on the journey, here are some learnings about growing and maintaining open source projects:

1. make videos sharing your OSS projects

videos, not tweets. this is probably my most important tip

i had a few viral tweets introducing my OSS projects that got lucky and had hundreds of thousands of views, but what brought in way more serious users and contributors was my youtube videos

good videos take a lot more effort to make, but it gives people a much more direct understanding of how your project works and how it delivers value. my hero project firstmate https://github.com/kunchenguid/firstmate grew largely due to my video content

make some videos. and make some more

2. use open source as a super power

i can't overstate how much better the tools got because of open source contributions from others. people bring great ideas, and test + fix the product in all kinds of edge cases that i can't possibly discover

in a way, an OSS product can guide itself towards PMF, because the community would collectively steer it towards the right direction

now that even non-developers can participate in contributing to OSS, this super power is becoming even stronger

3. set a minimum bar on contribution quality

the super power can also be a double edged sword here. especially with AI which allowed a lot more people to contribute but also lowered the bar. if left unchecked, you get a lot of noise

some projects outright disabled all PRs, while some others refuse to take anything done with AI. neither of which is the right approach IMO

my solution has been to raise the minimum bar by requiring all contributions to be raised through no-mistakes. it enforces a level of rigor, and slightly increases the cost to contribute so low quality noise would often shy away

i have a github action for enforcing this - https://github.com/kunchenguid/no-mistakes/tree/main/.github/actions/require-no-mistakes which you can use for your projects too

4. automate as much maintenance as possible

if you've contributed to my repos, you might have seen some of my automation at work. here's an example - https://github.com/kunchenguid/runner-up/pull/52 

i receive dozens, sometimes hundreds of incoming issues + PRs every day across my repos - i can't imagine how i could have kept all these projects moving if i hadn't leveraged agents to automate the triage work

i run the automation in grok bot with my firstmate bot there https://x.ai/bot/__4FfrkUdvpdMk6-LKg5r - it can set up a different bot per each repo, and creates the routines to triage incoming issues and PRs using cursor cloud agents according to my rules, yet allows me to talk to just the firstmate about everything

an important pre-requisite to doing that is a good documented vision for your project, which i write using https://github.com/kunchenguid/vision - with a clearly written vision statement, your triage agents can automatically rule out changes that don't align, and focus on the ones that would further the project towards the direction you want

i’ve been trying to get rid of adversarial reviews for quite a while now, but unfortunately every time i stopped it, i would find myself simply delaying the discovery of real problems, and the later i find them the more they cost

as a data point, i had measured how many real problems my adversarial reviewers actually caught, and it’s a lot.. 

that said, a good adversarial review setup is necessary for the ROI to be justifiable. i think a few things are very important:

1. original user intent must be explicitly collected (usually can be found in session transcripts where user inputs are) and passed to the reviewers 

2. there needs to be a human in the loop for ambiguous decisions. any scope change / expansion needs to escalated to the human user for decision

3. reviewers need to treat complexity like a disease and actively point out simplification opportunities 

4. reviewers need to challenge the lack of empirical evidence and hold the implementer accountable to prove their change

For 9 weeks, I mostly talked to one AI chat.
⠀
In that time, it finished 560+ tasks and merged 365 pull requests across my projects.
⠀
Yesterday, at Builder Sundays hosted at @Shopify's Ottawa office, I showed how. The tool is @myfirstmate, a free, open-source project by @kunchenguid, a former L8 engineer at Atlassian.
⠀
Kun built it because juggling parallel agent sessions was killing his focus. Every switch meant remembering what that session was about and what to do next. He didn't want a smarter workflow. He wanted the calm back, and the confidence that nothing falls through the cracks when you look away.
⠀
How it works: you are the captain, one agent acts as your firstmate, and a crew of agents does the work. Nothing goes live without your yes.
⠀
→ Orchestration. I only talk to firstmate. It breaks the work into separate tasks, starts a dedicated agent session for each one, and runs them in parallel. It keeps an eye on every session, handles the small stuff itself, and only comes to me when a decision actually needs me. When a task is done, it brings the result back for my review and approval.
⠀
→ Memory. It keeps my projects, rules and in-flight work. /bearings is my morning brief, /stow saves what it learned. I close the laptop and pick up tomorrow where I left off.
⠀
→ It improves itself. If something isn't working, I ask firstmate, and it fixes itself.
⠀
The result: Partexia went live on iOS and Android, and CrewTower shipped 23 releases.

Thank you Kun Chen for building this and sharing it with everyone.

quote.text:
now that we all agreed to not review most of the code any more, CI became the next bottleneck

at agent speed, if our CI pipeline is simply "run all the build, lint, tests", it'll become a major slow down

here are a few things i suggest for how to optimize:

1. balance load between CI and CD

CI protects main branch. CD protects production. if you can tolerate some delay in deploying your main branch to production, then you can do less in CI and do more in CD

for example, for a cross platform app i made my CI pipeline skip most mac and windows tests because linux already covered the same functionality

the tradeoff is occasionally i'd catch a mac or windows-only bug in CD before release, but in exchange, my CI pipeline became 15x faster - well worth it

2. modularize your codebase such that changes are isolated

then you can make your CI only run build, lint, test for the module being touched

this requires careful consideration for cross-module protocols. they should likely be their own modules, so when they do change, you know you probably need to test all dependent modules

3. for large modules, invest in test selection

in CI, try to only run tests that are covering the areas being changed. doing accurate test selection is not easy though, and often requires continuous tuning

i have a nightly loop specifically doing audit of past test runs and tweak my test selection to be more accurate. a big codebase of mine got pretty good at this - 20x faster CI compared to running all tests, and almost never miss any real problem

Tripwire @bot 

I built a security watcher grok bot. It's called Tripwire, and I just published it as a free template.

It doesn't spam you with every CVE. It learns your actual stack (repos, hosting, domains, accounts, devices) and only speaks up when something touches you.

What it watches:
- actively exploited vulns (CISA KEV, EPSS, NVD/GHSA, vendor advisories)
- certificate transparency for your domains, plus CA distrust events
- breaches for your emails and domains
- scams and lookalike domains
- leaked keys and permission creep in your bot setup

Skills it ships with:
- stack-inventory: a read-only map of your repos, hosting, domains, accounts, devices and bots
- vuln-triage: checks whether a new vuln or breach affects you, how urgent it is, and how to alert you
- cert-watch: certificate transparency, CA distrust, and lookalike domain checks
- incident-playbooks: the next 3 steps for a leaked key, an RCE, a bad dependency, a distrusted CA, a lost phone, an account takeover, phishing or prompt injection
- getting-started: a 5-question setup chat

How it works:
- confirms each item with two independent sources and labels rumors as unconfirmed
- critical issues come to you right away, any hour
- everything else goes into one quiet summary
- every alert says what happened, whether you're affected, the next 3 steps, and the deadline
- read-only everywhere, so it never patches or changes anything for you

It checks 3x a day and refreshes your inventory weekly. You get a Monday roundup, plus monthly device and backup checks and a quarterly 2FA audit.

interesting data from my most recent 2000 real tasks

all of these tasks' outcome got accepted by me, so consider them all successful. when a model didn't give me good results, i would get it to do more iterations until it succeeded

the main caveat is the "plan" bucket - if i didn't like a model's plan, i would sometimes just abandon it and it wouldn't show up here. sometimes i also explicitly ask astra / fable for difficult plans. so take the plan row with a grain of salt. the other rows are mostly randomized and fair

reasoning effort was set at xhigh for plan, medium for others

explaining the task types:
- research: these are mostly answering my questions
- plan: these are technical planning. it could be designing a new feature, or reproducing a bug
- implement: implementing an already defined spec
- fix: fix a bug that's already reproduced

a few interesting signals:

- sol 6.1 and sonnet 5.5 are almost exact equivalents, and they are both 5-10x more efficient at my implement and fix tasks than opus and astra

- grok 4.7 is efficient at read-only tasks, but quite expensive for writing code - this is likely because of its high price point for cached tokens so long coding sessions become very costly

- astra is a lot more expensive than opus 5.5, despite its token efficiency advantage. this is awkward because if sonnet matches sol, opus is better than astra, fable 5.5 is coming, and openai's subscription's $ value is getting cut in half, how do they compete?
